No time to compare alternatives

Less elastic supply

Necessarily negative

Close to zero
Necessarily greater than one
Necessarily negative

Unrelated to price
More elastic
More inelastic

options: An inferior good
A normal necessity with elasticity below one
A complement identified by cross-price elasticity
A normal luxury

before.q: Using the midpoint method, price for professional exam prep seats changes from $250 to $225 and quantity demanded changes from 400 to 480. What is price elasticity of demand?

after.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of a professional exam-prep course falls from $250 to $225, and quantity demanded rises from 400 seats to 480 seats. What is the price elasticity of demand?
after.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.73, so demand is elastic.

before.q: A public transit agency faces inelastic peak demand but elastic off-peak demand. Which change is most consistent with revenue management?

Cut peak fares and raise off-peak fares

after.q: A public transit agency faces inelastic peak demand but elastic off-peak demand. Which pricing strategy is most consistent with revenue management?
options: Raise peak fares and use discounts to attract off-peak riders
Cut peak fares and raise off-peak fares
Charge zero in both periods
Ignore elasticity because both services use the same buses
after.feedback: Higher prices fit the less elastic segment, while discounts can expand the more elastic segment.

before.q: A price floor creates a surplus. Which supply characteristic makes the surplus expand more strongly for a given price increase?

More inelastic supply

after.q: A price floor creates a surplus. All else equal, which supply characteristic would make the surplus larger for a given increase in price?
options: More elastic supply
More inelastic supply
Perfectly inelastic demand alone
A smaller number of sellers by itself
after.feedback: More elastic suppliers expand quantity supplied more in response to the supported price.

before.q: A firm raises price by about 6% and quantity demanded falls by about 3%. What should happen to total revenue, approximately?

after.q: A firm raises price by about 6% and quantity demanded falls by about 3%. What is the most likely effect on total revenue?
options: It cannot be inferred from percentage changes
It should rise because demand is inelastic over this range
It should fall because demand is elastic over this range
It should stay exactly constant because quantity changed

before.q: A regulator compares two identical per-unit fees. In Market X both curves are steep; in Market Y both are relatively flat. Which claim is best?
options: Market Y is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Market X is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss

Elasticity affects tax incidence but never deadweight loss

before.commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
before.feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

after.q: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
options: Reject the policy solely because one group loses
Assume there is no tradeoff because output rises
Evaluate only the change in total output.
Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
after.commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
after.feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

before.q: Scarcity exists when:
options: A seller earns a profit under the stated conditions.
Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
A store temporarily runs out of one item as the relevant economic conclusion.
A price is legally fixed for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Confusing scarcity with shortage or regulation.
before.feedback: Scarcity is the general condition of limited resources relative to wants.

after.q: Scarcity exists when:
options: A seller earns a profit
Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
A store temporarily runs out of one item
A price is legally fixed.
after.commonError: Confusing scarcity with shortage or regulation.
after.feedback: Scarcity is the general condition of limited resources relative to wants.

before.q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus under the stated conditions.
The end of scarcity in the situation described.
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee of equal benefits for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
before.feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

after.q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus
The end of scarcity
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee that everyone benefits equally.
after.commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
after.feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

before.q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a price shortage under the stated conditions.
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed after donations rise as the relevant economic conclusion.
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
before.feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

after.q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a temporary shortage
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed once donations increase
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases.
after.commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
after.feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

before.q: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which neighboring idea names the next-best use forgone?
options: Opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
Price elasticity
Monetary neutrality
before.commonError: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
before.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

after.q: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which concept names the next-best alternative forgone?
options: Opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
Price elasticity
Monetary neutrality
after.commonError: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
after.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

before.q: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which neighboring model displays the feasible combinations created by this scarcity?
options: A production possibilities frontier
A consumer price index
A money-demand curve
A Phillips curve
before.commonError: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
before.feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

after.q: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which model displays the feasible production combinations created by this scarcity?
options: A production possibilities frontier
A consumer price index
A money-demand curve
A Phillips curve
after.commonError: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
after.feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

before.q: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
options: $42,000 under the stated conditions.
$92,000 in the situation described.
$8,000 as the relevant economic conclusion.
$50,000 in forgone soybean output.
before.commonError: Using the difference rather than the value of the next-best alternative.
before.feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

after.q: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
options: $42,000, the value of the wheat that is chosen
$92,000, the combined value of wheat and soybeans
$8,000, the difference between the two crop values.
$50,000 in forgone soybean output.
after.commonError: Using the difference rather than the value of the next-best alternative.
after.feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

before.q: A government uses $20 million of idle-looking land for a courthouse. The land could be sold for $14 million or used for housing valued at $18 million. The opportunity cost is:
options: $32 million.
$20 million.
$14 million.
$18 million.
before.commonError: Using the purchase budget or adding rejected uses.
before.feedback: The housing project is the most valuable forgone use.

after.q: A government owns a vacant parcel valued on its books at $20 million and uses it for a courthouse. The land could instead be sold for $14 million or used for housing valued at $18 million. The opportunity cost is:
options: $32 million.
$20 million.
$14 million.
$18 million.
after.commonError: Using the purchase budget or adding rejected uses.
after.feedback: The housing project is the most valuable forgone use.

before.q: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
options: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price under the stated conditions.
The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated in the situation described.
The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost includes every possible future use added together for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Equating acquisition price with current opportunity cost.
before.feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

after.q: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
options: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price
The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated
The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost is the sum of the values of all possible future uses.
after.commonError: Equating acquisition price with current opportunity cost.
after.feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

before.q: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
options: The value of every available office.
$24,000 in forgone rent.
$0 because the space is owned.
The building’s original purchase price.
before.feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

after.q: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
options: The average rent of all comparable office spaces.
$24,000 in forgone rent.
$0 because the space is owned.
The building’s original purchase price.
after.feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

before.q: A farmer plants berries on land that could yield corn worth $48,000 or solar-lease income of $55,000. Berries are expected to net $62,000 after new expenses. What is the berries’ net benefit relative to their opportunity cost?
before.commonError: Comparing with the wrong land use or adding alternative returns.
before.feedback: The solar lease is the $55,000 opportunity cost; $62,000 minus $55,000 equals $7,000.

after.q: A farmer plants berries on land that could yield corn worth $48,000 or solar-lease income of $55,000. Berries are expected to net $62,000 after new expenses. Compared with the next-best use of the land, what is the net benefit of planting berries?
after.commonError: Comparing with the wrong land use or adding alternative returns.
after.feedback: The solar lease is the $55,000 opportunity cost; $62,000 minus $55,000 equals $7,000.

before.q: A free event can have an opportunity cost because:
options: Only paid activities have alternatives under the stated conditions.
Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
Past spending determines the cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Free events use no scarce resources for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
before.feedback: Time and other resources have alternative uses even when admission is free.

after.q: A free event can have an opportunity cost because:
options: Only paid activities have opportunity costs
Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
Past spending determines the opportunity cost of attending
Because the event is free, attending uses no scarce resources.
after.commonError: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
after.feedback: Time and other resources have alternative uses even when admission is free.

before.q: Scarcity means a community cannot fund every valued program. How does that fact create opportunity cost when it funds a clinic?
options: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
Scarcity makes the clinic’s historical spending a sunk cost
Opportunity cost disappears once officials approve a budget
Every unfunded program must be added together as the cost
before.commonError: Seeing scarcity and opportunity cost as unrelated definitions.
before.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost.

after.q: Scarcity means a community cannot fund every valued program. If the community funds a clinic, what determines the clinic’s opportunity cost?
options: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
Scarcity makes the clinic’s historical spending a sunk cost
Opportunity cost disappears once officials approve a budget
Every unfunded program must be added together as the cost
after.commonError: Seeing scarcity and opportunity cost as unrelated definitions.
after.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost.

before.q: A student has already paid a nonrefundable fee for a course. When deciding whether to continue, the fee should be treated as:
options: The opportunity cost of the next class meeting under the stated conditions.
A marginal benefit of continuing in the situation described.
A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
A reason to continue no matter what for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Letting an unrecoverable past cost control a current choice.
before.feedback: Only future benefits and future costs should guide the current decision.

after.q: A student has already paid a nonrefundable fee for a course. When deciding whether to continue, the fee should be treated as:
options: The opportunity cost of attending the next class meeting
A benefit of continuing because the fee has already been paid
A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
A reason to continue so the payment is not wasted.
after.commonError: Letting an unrecoverable past cost control a current choice.
after.feedback: Only future benefits and future costs should guide the current decision.

before.q: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $18 and its marginal cost is $14. The fourth unit should be:
options: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Rejected because total cost is positive in the situation described.
Accepted only if no sunk cost exists as the relevant economic conclusion.
Rejected unless average benefit also rises for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
before.feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

after.q: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $18 and its marginal cost is $14. The fourth unit should be:
options: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Rejected because any positive marginal cost makes the unit undesirable
Accepted only if no sunk costs were incurred earlier
Rejected unless average benefit also rises.
after.commonError: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
after.feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

before.q: A firm has already spent $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to generate $18,000. The firm should:
options: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000 under the stated conditions.
Finish only to avoid wasting the $50,000 in the situation described.
Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
Ignore the expected revenue because it is uncertain for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
before.feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

after.q: A firm has already spent $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to generate $18,000. The firm should:
options: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000
Finish so the original $50,000 is not wasted
Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
Ignore the $18,000 expected revenue because it is uncertain.
after.commonError: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
after.feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

before.q: A museum stays open an extra hour. The added admissions revenue is $900 and added staffing and utility cost is $1,100. Marginal analysis says:
options: Stay open because total daily revenue is high under the stated conditions.
Stay open to recover fixed building costs in the situation described.
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
before.feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

after.q: A museum stays open an extra hour. The added admissions revenue is $900 and added staffing and utility cost is $1,100. Marginal analysis says:
options: Stay open because total daily revenue is high
Stay open to recover fixed building costs
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises.
after.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
after.feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

before.q: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
options: Accept to spread fixed costs as the relevant economic conclusion.
Accept because average profit is positive in the situation described.
Accept because total revenue will rise as the relevant economic conclusion.
Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
before.commonError: Using average profitability to justify a negative marginal transaction.
before.feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

after.q: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
options: Accept the customer to spread fixed costs over more customers
Accept because average profit is positive
Accept because total revenue will increase.
Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
after.commonError: Using average profitability to justify a negative marginal transaction.
after.feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

before.q: A project already cost $8 million. Finishing costs $5 million. Expected future benefits are $4 million, but cancellation requires a $0.5 million cleanup cost. What is the best choice?
options: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
Finish because future benefits exceed cleanup cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Cancel because total project cost exceeds total benefit as the relevant economic conclusion.
Finish to avoid wasting the $8 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
before.commonError: Ignoring the relevant alternatives after a sunk cost.
before.feedback: Compare future choices: finish yields -$1 million; cancel costs $0.5 million.

after.q: A project already cost $8 million. Finishing costs $5 million. Expected future benefits are $4 million, but cancellation requires a $0.5 million cleanup cost. What is the best choice?
options: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
Finish because future benefits exceed the $0.5 million cleanup cost
Cancel because total project cost exceeds total benefit
Finish so the $8 million already spent is not wasted.
after.commonError: Ignoring the relevant alternatives after a sunk cost.
after.feedback: Compare future choices: finish yields -$1 million; cancel costs $0.5 million.

before.q: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. What should the firm do?
options: Abandon both options because total spending is already too high as the relevant economic conclusion.
Finish to recover the $12 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
Sell the unfinished prototype because finishing produces $1 million less than the current alternative.
Finish because $6 million exceeds $1.5 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
before.commonError: Comparing gross future revenue without considering the alternative and remaining cost.
before.feedback: Finishing nets -$1 million relative to now, while selling the prototype yields $1.5 million.

after.q: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. What should the firm do?
options: Abandon the project because total spending is already too high
Finish so the $12 million already spent is not wasted
Sell the unfinished prototype because finishing produces $1 million less than the current alternative.
Finish because $6 million exceeds the $1.5 million sale value of the unfinished prototype.
after.commonError: Comparing gross future revenue without considering the alternative and remaining cost.
after.feedback: Finishing nets -$1 million relative to now, while selling the prototype yields $1.5 million.

before.q: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. What is the best marginal choice?
options: End the policy because $30 million is less costly than an $80 million negative continuation margin.
End because total cost exceeds total benefit since inception as the relevant economic conclusion.
Continue to avoid wasting the $2 billion as the relevant economic conclusion.
Continue because benefits exceed transition costs as the relevant economic conclusion.
before.commonError: Letting sunk spending or an irrelevant total comparison drive the decision.
before.feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

after.q: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. What is the best marginal choice?
options: End the policy because $30 million is less costly than an $80 million negative continuation margin.
End because total cost since the program began exceeds total benefit
Continue so the $2 billion already spent is not wasted
Continue because the $520 million in benefits exceeds the $30 million transition cost.
after.commonError: Letting sunk spending or an irrelevant total comparison drive the decision.
after.feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

before.q: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefit, costs firms $3.6 million, and prevents recreation worth $1.5 million. What is the social marginal choice?
options: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
before.commonError: Ignoring a relevant external or opportunity cost.
before.feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

after.q: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefits, costs firms $3.6 million, and reduces recreational value by $1.5 million. Based on social marginal analysis, should the additional reduction be required?
options: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
after.commonError: Ignoring a relevant external or opportunity cost.
after.feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

before.q: A nonprofit can deliver one more meal route. Donations attributable to the route are $900, food and fuel cost $620, and volunteer time displaces tutoring worth $310. What is the choice?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high
before.commonError: Treating unpaid resources as zero marginal cost.
before.feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

after.q: A nonprofit is considering one more meal-delivery route. The route would generate $900 in attributable donations, cost $620 for food and fuel, and use volunteer time that would otherwise provide tutoring worth $310. Should the nonprofit add the route?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high
after.commonError: Treating unpaid resources as zero marginal cost.
after.feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

before.q: A grocer can stock one more crate. Expected sales margin is $45, spoilage risk costs $12, and shelf labor costs $18. What should the grocer do?
options: Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
Reject it because spoilage risk makes total benefit uncertain
Stock it only if the store’s average profit increases
Reject it because both cost items must be added to revenue
before.commonError: Ignoring a cost component or adding benefit and cost.
before.feedback: Marginal cost is $30, leaving $15 in net marginal benefit.

after.q: A grocer can stock one more crate. Expected sales margin is $45, spoilage risk costs $12, and shelf labor costs $18. What should the grocer do?
options: Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
Reject it because spoilage risk makes total benefit uncertain
Stock it only if the store’s average profit increases
Reject it because adding the crate increases total store costs.
after.commonError: Ignoring a cost component or adding benefit and cost.
after.feedback: Marginal cost is $30, leaving $15 in net marginal benefit.

before.q: The marginal rule says to continue while:
options: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average cost is falling in the situation described.
Total benefit is positive as the relevant economic conclusion.
Past spending is large for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Using totals, averages, or sunk costs.
before.feedback: The next unit should be chosen when its added benefit covers its added cost.

after.q: The marginal rule says to continue while:
options: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average cost is falling
Total benefit is positive
Past spending is large.
after.commonError: Using totals, averages, or sunk costs.
after.feedback: The next unit should be chosen when its added benefit covers its added cost.

before.q: A tax credit for home improvements is claimed by many households that would have renovated anyway. What weakens the policy’s effect?
options: The credit has no budget cost.
A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.
Households never respond to prices.
The policy creates a price floor.
before.commonError: Counting subsidized activity as caused by the subsidy.
before.feedback: An incentive is effective at the margin only when it changes decisions that otherwise would differ.

after.q: A tax credit for home improvements is claimed by many households that would have renovated anyway. Why might the credit generate relatively little additional renovation?
options: The credit has no budget cost.
A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.
Households never respond to prices.
The policy creates a price floor.
after.commonError: Counting subsidized activity as caused by the subsidy.
after.feedback: An incentive is effective at the margin only when it changes decisions that otherwise would differ.

before.q: A given penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
options: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.
before.feedback: A fixed incentive can have different marginal importance for different decision-makers.

after.q: The same dollar penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
options: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.
after.feedback: A fixed incentive can have different marginal importance for different decision-makers.

before.q: A minimum wage is above equilibrium. Firms respond by cutting hours, raising hiring standards, and using more automation. What principle is being tested?
options: People and firms respond to incentives on multiple margins
Price floors eliminate tradeoffs
Higher wages always increase labor demanded
The wage floor is nonbinding if any workers are hired
before.feedback: A wage floor changes incentives, so firms can adjust through hiring, hours, standards, prices, or technology.

after.q: A minimum wage is above equilibrium. Firms respond by cutting hours, raising hiring standards, and using more automation. Which economic principle best explains these responses?
options: People and firms respond to incentives on multiple margins
Price floors eliminate tradeoffs
Higher wages always increase labor demanded
The wage floor is nonbinding if any workers are hired
after.feedback: A wage floor changes incentives, so firms can adjust through hiring, hours, standards, prices, or technology.

before.q: A subsidy for electric cars increases purchases, but also mostly benefits households who would have bought electric cars anyway. What idea is being tested?
options: Incentives can create intended responses and unintended distributional effects
Subsidies remove scarcity
A subsidy is the same as a binding price ceiling
Consumers ignore incentives when products are expensive
before.feedback: Incentives change behavior, but the actual benefits may not land exactly where policymakers intended.

after.q: A subsidy for electric cars increases purchases, but also mostly benefits households who would have bought electric cars anyway. Which interpretation best describes this outcome?
options: Incentives can create intended responses and unintended distributional effects
Subsidies remove scarcity
A subsidy is the same as a binding price ceiling
Consumers ignore incentives when products are expensive
after.feedback: Incentives change behavior, but the actual benefits may not land exactly where policymakers intended.

before.q: A sports contract pays a large bonus for games played. An injured athlete returns early and performs poorly. What is the careful conclusion?
options: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome
The poor performance proves the bonus was not an incentive
Bonuses influence effort but never participation decisions
Playing establishes that the athlete approved of the contract design
before.commonError: Equating a behavioral response with a desirable or certain result.
before.feedback: The bonus changed the payoff to participation, while health and performance remained uncertain.

after.q: A sports contract pays a large bonus for games played. An injured athlete returns early and performs poorly. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome
The poor performance proves the bonus was not an incentive
Bonuses influence effort but never participation decisions
Playing establishes that the athlete approved of the contract design
after.commonError: Equating a behavioral response with a desirable or certain result.
after.feedback: The bonus changed the payoff to participation, while health and performance remained uncertain.

before.q: Remote work lowers commuting time for an employee, making a job offer more attractive even though salary is unchanged. What created the incentive response?
options: A lower opportunity cost of accepting the job
A cash bonus hidden in the salary
A guaranteed increase in job satisfaction
Moral approval of remote work
before.commonError: Looking only for explicit cash rewards and missing a changed alternative cost.
before.feedback: Reduced commuting time changes the relative cost of choosing the job.

after.q: Remote work lowers commuting time for an employee, making a job offer more attractive even though salary is unchanged. Why can this change make the job more attractive?
options: A lower opportunity cost of accepting the job
A cash bonus hidden in the salary
A guaranteed increase in job satisfaction
Moral approval of remote work
after.commonError: Looking only for explicit cash rewards and missing a changed alternative cost.
after.feedback: Reduced commuting time changes the relative cost of choosing the job.

before.q: A professor adds one point for each discussion post. How does marginal analysis connect to the incentive students face?
options: The extra point raises the marginal benefit of one more post
The total course grade becomes the cost of every post
Scarcity disappears once points are available
The added point guarantees that every post improves learning
before.commonError: Missing that an incentive changes the next action’s marginal payoff.
before.feedback: The added point changes the marginal benefit of submitting another post; quality is a separate outcome.

after.q: A professor adds one point for each discussion post. How does the extra point affect the marginal decision to make one more post?
options: The extra point raises the marginal benefit of one more post
The total course grade becomes the cost of every post
Scarcity disappears once points are available
The added point guarantees that every post improves learning
after.commonError: Missing that an incentive changes the next action’s marginal payoff.
after.feedback: The added point changes the marginal benefit of submitting another post; quality is a separate outcome.

before.q: A policy aims to reduce congestion but rewards agencies only for bus tickets sold. What lesson connects incentives to policy design?
options: The rewarded measure may redirect behavior away from the stated policy objective
A stated goal automatically determines the behavioral margin
Ticket sales are identical to reduced congestion
An incentive exists only after congestion falls
before.commonError: Confusing a stated purpose, measured target, and final outcome.
before.feedback: Policy design must align the payoff with the behavior and outcome actually sought.

after.q: A policy aims to reduce congestion but rewards agencies only for bus tickets sold. What problem can this funding rule create?
options: The rewarded measure may redirect behavior away from the stated policy objective
A stated goal automatically determines the behavioral margin
Ticket sales are identical to reduced congestion
An incentive exists only after congestion falls
after.commonError: Confusing a stated purpose, measured target, and final outcome.
after.feedback: Policy design must align the payoff with the behavior and outcome actually sought.

before.q: One inflation model studies demand pressure; another studies supply disruptions. Which should be used after an energy shock?
options: The model containing the relevant supply mechanism
The model with the most equations on the page
Whichever model predicts the preferred policy
Both models averaged without checking assumptions
before.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
before.feedback: An energy shock operates through supply costs, making the supply-disruption model the more relevant mechanism.

after.q: One inflation model studies demand pressure; another studies supply disruptions. Which should be used after an energy shock?
options: The model containing the relevant supply mechanism
The model with the most equations on the page
Whichever model predicts the preferred policy

options: No, because one seller has market power
Yes, because many buyers are enough
Yes, because all markets are competitive
No, because buyers never matter

options: No, because one seller has market power
Yes, because many buyers are enough
Yes, because all markets are competitive
No, because buyers never matter
after.feedback: A competitive market requires many buyers and sellers, with no single participant controlling price.

before.q: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What is the likely firm-level demand condition?

Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
Buyers cannot compare offers.
An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.

after.q: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What does this imply about an individual seller’s ability to set price?
options: Each seller controls market demand.
Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
Buyers cannot compare offers.
An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.
after.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.

before.q: Two goods are complements when:
options: They are commonly used together
They can always replace one another
Both are price ceilings
Neither has demand

after.q: Two goods are complements when:
options: They are commonly used together
One good can be used in place of the other
The goods are produced using the same inputs
A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unchanged.
after.feedback: Complements are goods used together.

before.q: The market moves from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve. What is the most precise description?

Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.
Price falls, causing quantity demanded to decrease along D.
Supply increases, shifting S to the right.

It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand

As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As supply rises, demand must rise

As price falls, demand shifts left
As price rises, quantity demanded rises

Quantity supplied changes
The market moves along demand

The good's own price changes

A change in the good's own price
A change in quantity demanded
A movement along the demand curve.

Higher price; less quantity supplied along S.
More demand; D shifts to the right.
Higher price; more quantity supplied along S.

after.q: Points A and B lie on one supply curve. What economic change occurs between them?

Price rises, causing quantity supplied to decrease along S.

75 thousand units
200 thousand units
100 thousand units

As price rises, supply shifts left
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As demand rises, supply must rise

As price rises, supply shifts left
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As demand rises, supply must rise

Demand decreases
Supply increases

after.q: Steel becomes more expensive for car producers. What happens to the supply of cars?

Quantity supplied increases because car price changed
Demand decreases
Supply increases

Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases

options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases
after.feedback: The repair cue identifies steel as an input. A higher input price raises marginal production cost and shifts car supply left.

before.q: The cost of steel rises for car producers. What happens to car supply?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases

after.q: The cost of steel rises for car producers. What happens to car supply?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases
after.feedback: Higher steel costs make each quantity of cars more expensive to produce, reducing supply and shifting the supply curve left.

It disappears

after.q: If supply increases and demand does not change, what happens to equilibrium price?
options: It decreases
It increases
It remains unchanged because demand did not change.
It increases because more units are available for sale.
after.feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.

after.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. The market begins at D1 and S1. Supply then increases, followed by an increase in demand. What is the final equilibrium?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
after.feedback: Starting at D1 and S1 gives P2, Q1. A supply increase moves equilibrium to P1, Q2. Then a demand increase moves equilibrium to P2, Q3.

options: Equilibrium moves from Q2/P3 to Q3/P2
Equilibrium moves from Q1/P2 to Q2/P3
Equilibrium moves from Q2/P1 to Q3/P2
Equilibrium moves from Q3/P2 to Q2/P1
before.feedback: A supply increase shifts supply right from S1 to S2, lowering price and raising quantity.

after.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2.
after.feedback: A supply increase shifts supply right from S1 to S2, lowering price and raising quantity.

before.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from Q2/P1 to Q1/P2
Equilibrium moves from Q1/P2 to Q2/P1
Equilibrium moves from Q3/P2 to Q2/P3
Equilibrium moves from Q2/P3 to Q3/P2
before.feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.

after.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Evaluate the move from D1/S1 to D2/S2 by separating what simultaneous demand and supply increases imply in general from what the displayed intersections establish here.
options: Quantity rises generally; price is ambiguous generally but stays at P2 here as quantity moves from Q1 to Q3
Price rises generally; quantity is ambiguous generally but stays at Q1 here as price moves from P1 to P3
Both variables are ambiguous generally, and the graph shows both unchanged
Quantity falls generally; price is ambiguous generally but falls to P1 here

after.q: Refer to the graph. Demand and supply both increase from D1/S1 to D2/S2. What does economic theory predict in general, and what does this particular graph show?
options: Quantity rises generally; price is ambiguous generally but stays at P2 here as quantity moves from Q1 to Q3
Price rises generally; quantity is ambiguous generally but stays at Q1 here as price moves from P1 to P3
Both variables are ambiguous generally, and the graph shows both unchanged
Quantity falls generally; price is ambiguous generally but falls to P1 here
after.feedback: Both shifts raise quantity. Their price effects oppose, so price is indeterminate without magnitudes; this graph supplies those magnitudes and shows the price effects offset at P2.

before.q: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. What outcome is certain if both effects are strong but unknown in size?

Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises

after.q: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
after.feedback: Demand increases and supply decreases. Both raise price, but quantity depends on which shift is larger.

before.q: A hurricane destroys supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today's market?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises

after.q: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
after.feedback: Expected future price increases raise current demand, while the hurricane lowers supply. Price rises; quantity is ambiguous.

before.q: Demand increases while supply stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises

after.q: Demand increases while supply stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
after.feedback: The demand increase moves the market to a higher point on the unchanged supply curve, raising both equilibrium price and quantity.

before.q: At a market checkpoint, demand shifts right while supply shifts left at the same time. Which equilibrium change can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price falls
before.feedback: Demand rising and supply falling both push price up, but quantity depends on which shift is stronger.

after.q: Demand shifts right while supply shifts left at the same time. Which equilibrium change can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price falls
after.feedback: Demand rising and supply falling both push price up, but quantity depends on which shift is stronger.

before.q: An economist observes inventories accumulating. What is a surplus?

A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A point outside the PPF
A legal maximum price

after.q: Inventories are accumulating because sellers are offering more units than buyers want at the current price. What market condition exists?
options: A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A point outside the PPF
A legal maximum price
after.feedback: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Easy
entries.concept: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

before.q: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
options: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore
before.commonError: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
before.feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

after.q: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
options: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient.
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore
after.commonError: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
after.feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Easy
entries.concept: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

before.q: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
options: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange
before.commonError: Inferring comparative advantage from productivity alone.
before.feedback: Greater output from the same resources establishes absolute, not necessarily comparative, advantage.

after.q: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
options: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop.
West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange
after.commonError: Inferring comparative advantage from productivity alone.
after.feedback: Greater output from the same resources establishes absolute, not necessarily comparative, advantage.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Easy
entries.concept: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

before.q: One worker can finish more of both tasks than a coworker. Why might the coworker still specialize in one task?
options: The coworker may have the lower opportunity cost in that task
The faster worker loses absolute advantage after delegation under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Comparative advantage requires equal productivity
Specialization removes every tradeoff
before.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
before.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

after.q: One worker can finish more of both tasks than a coworker. Why might the coworker still specialize in one task?
options: The coworker may have the lower opportunity cost in that task
The faster worker should perform both tasks because they produce more of each.
Comparative advantage requires equal productivity
Specialization removes every tradeoff
after.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
after.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Easy
entries.concept: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

before.q: Why can specialization according to comparative advantage expand what two producers can consume?
options: It can increase combined production available for exchange
It guarantees each producer makes every good under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
It makes opportunity costs identical
It removes scarcity from both producers
before.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
before.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

after.q: Why can specialization according to comparative advantage expand what two producers can consume?
options: It can increase combined production available for exchange
It guarantees each producer can make every good more efficiently.
It makes opportunity costs identical
It removes scarcity from both producers
after.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
after.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Medium

before.q: Team A can prepare 12 briefs or 6 charts daily. Team B can prepare 8 briefs or 8 charts. Who has comparative advantage in briefs?
options: Team A; one brief costs 0.5 chart rather than 1 chart
Team B; it can make more charts under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Team A; it has comparative advantage in both outputs
Neither; their maximum outputs differ
before.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
before.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

after.q: Team A can prepare 12 briefs or 6 charts daily. Team B can prepare 8 briefs or 8 charts. Who has comparative advantage in briefs?
options: Team A; one brief costs 0.5 chart rather than 1 chart
Team B; it can make more charts.
Team A; it has comparative advantage in both outputs
Neither; their maximum outputs differ
after.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
after.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

before.q: If one mug costs a studio 2 bowls, what is the reciprocal opportunity cost of one bowl?

Two mugs under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Four mugs
One mug

before.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

after.q: If one mug costs a studio 2 bowls, what is the reciprocal opportunity cost of one bowl?
options: One-half mug
Two mugs.
Four mugs
One mug
after.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
after.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

before.q: Two workshops each give up exactly 3 frames to produce one desk. What does the basic model imply?
options: Neither has comparative advantage in desks based on these costs
The workshop with greater desk output must specialize in desks under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Both receive strict gains from any desk price
One workshop must have comparative advantage in both goods
before.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
before.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

after.q: Two workshops each give up exactly 3 frames to produce one desk. What does the basic model imply?
options: Neither has comparative advantage in desks based on these costs
The workshop with greater desk output must specialize in desks.
Both receive strict gains from any desk price
One workshop must have comparative advantage in both goods
after.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
after.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Hard
entries.concept: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

before.q: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
options: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident
before.commonError: Preferring self-sufficiency without comparing opportunity costs.
before.feedback: Exchange uses resources worth 3 tons rather than 5, freeing 2 tons for other uses.

after.q: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
options: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade.
The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident
after.commonError: Preferring self-sufficiency without comparing opportunity costs.
after.feedback: Exchange uses resources worth 3 tons rather than 5, freeing 2 tons for other uses.

entries.questionSet: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade - Hard

before.q: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?

Comparative advantage is false whenever gains are unequal under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output

before.feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

after.q: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
Comparative advantage is disproved whenever gains are unequal.
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output
after.commonError: Confusing total gains with mutual benefit under a particular exchange.
after.feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs

after.q: Ava’s cost of one crate is 2 sacks; Ben’s is 5 sacks. At exactly 2 sacks per crate, which statement is correct?
options: Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
Both receive strict gains from the trade.
Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs

Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only

options: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt

Sellers bear 2 dollars, proving perfectly elastic supply
Buyers remit it, bear 6 dollars, and are less elastic

before.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

after.q: Refer to the graph. The tax is legally imposed on buyers. Which statement correctly describes who remits the tax, who bears the economic burden, and what the burden split implies about elasticity?

before.q: Demand is perfectly inelastic and supply slopes upward. Who bears a per-unit tax?
options: Buyers bear essentially all of it
Sellers bear essentially all of it
The burden is split equally
No one bears it because quantity is fixed
before.feedback: With perfectly inelastic demand, buyers do not reduce quantity, so the buyer price rises by the tax.

after.q: Demand is perfectly inelastic and supply slopes upward. Who bears a per-unit tax?
options: Buyers bear all of it.
Sellers bear essentially all of it
The burden is split equally
No one bears it because quantity is fixed
after.feedback: With perfectly inelastic demand, quantity demanded does not respond to price. The buyer price therefore rises by the full amount of the tax, so buyers bear the entire burden.

before.q: The less elastic side of the market usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Only the legal paperwork
before.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

after.q: The less elastic side of the market usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Only the portion of the tax named in the statute.
after.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.
