before.q: A tax on cigarettes reduces smoking less than expected but raises substantial revenue. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Supply increased after the tax
The tax created a price floor
before.feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

after.q: A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in smoking even though buyers face a noticeably higher price. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Supply increased after the tax
The tax created a price floor
after.feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

before.q: After a binding rent ceiling is imposed, some landlords move units into unregulated short-term rentals. Which lesson about price controls follows?
options: A policy can change incentives and reduce quantity supplied in the regulated market
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied, because one vocabulary label resolves every consequence
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
before.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

after.q: After a binding rent ceiling is imposed, some landlords move units into unregulated short-term rentals. Which lesson about price controls follows?
options: A policy can change incentives and reduce quantity supplied in the regulated market
A ceiling increases quantity supplied because landlords must meet the stronger demand at the lower price.
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
after.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

before.q: Suppose an equal per-unit tax could legally be collected from either buyers or sellers. In the standard supply-demand model, why is the equilibrium incidence similar either way?
options: Only buyer taxes reduce quantity, without tracing the combined incentives and tradeoffs
Either tax creates the same wedge between buyer price and seller price
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
before.feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

after.q: Suppose an equal per-unit tax could legally be collected from either buyers or sellers. In the standard supply-demand model, why is the equilibrium incidence similar either way?
options: Only a buyer tax reduces quantity because it directly affects demand.
Either tax creates the same wedge between buyer price and seller price
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
after.feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

before.q: A company pays bonuses for speed. Output rises, but quality complaints increase. What does this show?
options: Incentives do not affect workers, without tracing the combined incentives and tradeoffs
Marginal analysis requires ignoring quality
Incentives work, but poorly designed incentives can distort behavior
The policy created a price ceiling
before.feedback: People respond to the measured incentive, which can improve one outcome while damaging another.

after.q: A company pays bonuses for speed. Output rises, but quality complaints increase. What does this show?
options: Incentives do not affect workers because quality is separate from the bonus.
Marginal analysis requires ignoring quality
Incentives work, but poorly designed incentives can distort behavior
The policy created a price ceiling
after.feedback: People respond to the measured incentive, which can improve one outcome while damaging another.

before.q: A price-ceiling model predicts a shortage. In practice, the city also sees black markets, quality cuts, and favoritism. What does that comparison reveal about economic models?
options: The model captures the core shortage logic, while real-world institutions shape how the shortage appears
The model is useless because it did not list every consequence
The model proves black markets cannot happen, while ignoring the second mechanism in the scenario
The model becomes normative once real examples are added
before.feedback: A simple model explains the core mechanism. Real-world details determine the specific form the shortage takes.

after.q: A price-ceiling model predicts a shortage. In practice, the city also sees black markets, quality cuts, and favoritism. What does that comparison reveal about economic models?
options: The model captures the core shortage logic, while real-world institutions shape how the shortage appears
The model is useless because it did not list every consequence
The model proves black markets cannot happen because the legal price is fixed.
The model becomes normative once real examples are added
after.feedback: A simple model explains the core mechanism. Real-world details determine the specific form the shortage takes.

before.q: A price ceiling is imposed during an inflation spike. Official prices stop rising, but buyers wait longer and pay side fees. What is the best interpretation?
options: Inflation is fully eliminated because the listed price cannot rise
The legal money price is capped, but the full cost to buyers may still rise
The good becomes less scarce, while ignoring the second mechanism in the scenario
The CPI must perfectly capture waiting time
before.feedback: A price ceiling can hide costs in waiting time, side payments, lower quality, or black markets.

after.q: A price ceiling is imposed during an inflation spike. Official prices stop rising, but buyers wait longer and pay side fees. What is the best interpretation?
options: Inflation is fully eliminated because the listed price cannot rise
The posted price is capped, but the full economic cost to buyers may still rise.
The good becomes less scarce because the posted price is lower.
The CPI must perfectly capture waiting time
after.feedback: A price ceiling can hide costs in waiting time, side payments, lower quality, or black markets.

before.q: The unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching. What should a student conclude?
options: The labor market definitely improved because a lower unemployment rate is always good
The labor market may not have improved even though the official unemployment rate fell
The economy must have higher productivity
The CPI must have fallen
before.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

after.q: The unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: The labor market definitely improved because a lower unemployment rate is always good
The labor market may not have improved even though the official unemployment rate fell
The economy must have higher productivity
The CPI must have fallen
after.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

before.q: A tax is legally placed on buyers instead of sellers. What should students remember from tax incidence?
options: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market
before.feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

after.q: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
options: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market
after.feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

before.q: An economist asks which side bears more of a tax burden when demand is less elastic than supply.
options: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
before.feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

after.q: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
options: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
after.feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

before.q: “Holding the money price below equilibrium does not erase scarcity; it changes how scarcity is rationed.” What does this mean?
options: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change
before.feedback: A ceiling can hold down the legal money price, but scarcity still appears through shortages and nonprice rationing.

after.q: A binding price ceiling holds the posted price below equilibrium. What happens to the underlying scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change
after.feedback: A ceiling can hold down the legal money price, but scarcity still appears through shortages and nonprice rationing.

before.q: A country has more machines per worker, but each additional machine adds less extra output than the one before. What concept is being tested?
options: Substitution bias
Frictional unemployment
A binding price ceiling
Diminishing returns to capital
before.feedback: Diminishing returns means each additional unit of capital adds less extra output once capital is already abundant.

after.q: A country has more machines per worker, but each additional machine adds less extra output than the one before. What explains this pattern?
options: Substitution bias
Frictional unemployment
A binding price ceiling
Diminishing returns to capital
after.feedback: Diminishing returns means each additional unit of capital adds less extra output once capital is already abundant.

before.q: An economist asks: a policy boosts productivity over time but temporarily displaces workers in old industries. Which answer best synthesizes the issue?
options: Long-run growth can coexist with short-run structural unemployment
Productivity growth means no one ever loses a job
Structural unemployment only happens when CPI rises
Worker displacement proves the economy cannot grow
before.feedback: Productivity growth can raise long-run living standards while creating short-run adjustment costs for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

after.q: A policy raises productivity over time but temporarily displaces workers in old industries. Which statement best describes the tradeoff?
options: Long-run growth can coexist with short-run structural unemployment
Productivity growth means no one ever loses a job
Structural unemployment only happens when CPI rises
Worker displacement proves the economy cannot grow
after.feedback: Productivity growth can raise long-run living standards while creating short-run adjustment costs for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

before.q: An economist places a tax on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
options: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement
before.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

after.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
options: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement
after.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

before.q: Why can one country support higher wages and living standards over time? Which answer best connects economic choice and productivity growth?
options: Higher productivity allows workers to produce more output per hour
Higher nominal prices automatically create more real wealth
A price ceiling always increases available goods
Unemployment insurance directly raises productivity
before.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity, meaning output produced per worker or per hour.

after.q: Which factor best explains how a country can support higher wages and living standards over time?
options: Higher productivity allows workers to produce more output per hour
Higher nominal prices automatically create more real wealth
A price ceiling always increases available goods
Unemployment insurance directly raises productivity
after.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity, meaning output produced per worker or per hour.

before.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 4.8%, but employment does not increase and labor-force participation falls sharply. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The labor market definitely improved because the unemployment rate fell
Productivity must have increased because unemployment fell, while treating a policy prediction as a value conclusion
Inflation must have fallen because labor-force participation fell
The labor market may be weaker than the unemployment rate suggests because people exited the labor force
before.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

after.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 4.8%, but employment does not increase and labor-force participation falls sharply. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The labor market definitely improved because the unemployment rate fell
Productivity must have increased because the unemployment rate fell.
Inflation must have fallen because labor-force participation fell
The labor market may be weaker than the unemployment rate suggests because people exited the labor force
after.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if people stop looking for work and leave the labor force.

before.q: A recession ends. Some discouraged workers begin searching again before finding jobs. What can happen to the unemployment rate and why?
options: It can rise temporarily because people reenter the labor force and are counted as unemployed while searching
It must fall because reentering workers are automatically employed
It must stay constant because discouraged workers were already unemployed
It can rise only if CPI rises, without checking how the component effects interact
before.feedback: When discouraged workers resume searching, they reenter the labor force and may be counted as unemployed until they find jobs.

after.q: A recession ends. Some discouraged workers begin searching again before finding jobs. What can happen to the unemployment rate and why?
options: It can rise temporarily because people reenter the labor force and are counted as unemployed while searching
It must fall because reentering workers are automatically employed
It must stay constant because discouraged workers were already unemployed
It can rise only if employment falls.
after.feedback: When discouraged workers resume searching, they reenter the labor force and may be counted as unemployed until they find jobs.

before.q: A binding price ceiling causes landlords to reduce maintenance. Rent is cheaper for lucky tenants, but housing quality falls. What concept combination is being tested?
options: Tax incidence and real interest rates
Catch-up growth and discouraged workers
Price control incentives and CPI quality-measurement limits
GDP final-goods accounting and nominal wages
before.feedback: A lower legal price can come with worse quality, and quality changes are one reason cost-of-living measurement gets messy.

after.q: A binding price ceiling causes landlords to reduce maintenance. Rent is cheaper for lucky tenants, but housing quality falls. Which pair of concepts best explains these effects?
options: Tax incidence and real interest rates
Catch-up growth and discouraged workers
Price control incentives and CPI quality-measurement limits
GDP final-goods accounting and nominal wages
after.feedback: A lower legal price can come with worse quality, and quality changes are one reason cost-of-living measurement gets messy.

before.q: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which answer best avoids the trap?
options: Automation must reduce living standards because some workers lose jobs
Automation eliminates unemployment because output rises, because one vocabulary label resolves every consequence
Automation only affects CPI and not labor markets
Productivity can improve long-run living standards while causing short-run structural unemployment
before.feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.

after.q: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
options: Automation must reduce living standards because some workers lose jobs
Automation eliminates unemployment because higher output creates jobs for every displaced worker.
Automation only affects CPI and not labor markets
Productivity can improve long-run living standards while causing short-run structural unemployment
after.feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.

before.q: A supply shock raises food prices. The government caps prices below equilibrium. Official prices rise less, but shortages emerge, quality falls, and households spend more time searching. What is the best synthesis?
options: The ceiling eliminates inflation and improves allocation because prices are lower
The ceiling suppresses posted prices but worsens allocation and hides part of the full cost of scarcity
The ceiling creates a surplus and raises producer incentives, because mentioning two concepts completes the causal analysis
The ceiling shifts demand left because consumers want more food
before.feedback: A ceiling can reduce the posted price while causing shortages, lower quality, waiting costs, and misallocation.

after.q: A supply shock raises food prices. The government caps prices below equilibrium. Official prices rise less, but shortages emerge, quality falls, and households spend more time searching. What is the best synthesis?
options: The ceiling eliminates inflation and improves allocation because prices are lower
The ceiling suppresses posted prices but worsens allocation and hides part of the full cost of scarcity
The ceiling creates a surplus because the lower price encourages producers to supply more.
The ceiling shifts demand left because consumers want more food
after.feedback: A ceiling can reduce the posted price while causing shortages, lower quality, waiting costs, and misallocation.

before.q: The final Market Marshal trap: unemployment falls, CPI inflation slows because price ceilings cap posted prices, real wages appear stable, and productivity is flat. Which warning is most important?
options: The economy is clearly stronger because unemployment and CPI inflation both fell
Stable real wages prove productivity increased, because mentioning two concepts completes the causal analysis
Price ceilings improve welfare whenever inflation slows, while treating a policy prediction as a value conclusion
The indicators may be distorted by labor-force exits, hidden price-control costs, and lack of productivity growth
before.feedback: Headline indicators can mislead. Falling unemployment may reflect labor-force exits, capped prices may hide shortages, and flat productivity weakens long-run living standards.

after.q: The Market Marshal presents a final scenario: unemployment falls, CPI inflation slows because price ceilings cap posted prices, real wages appear stable, and productivity is flat. Which warning is most important?
options: The economy is clearly stronger because unemployment and CPI inflation both fell
Stable real wages prove productivity increased because purchasing power did not fall.
Price ceilings improve welfare whenever they slow posted-price inflation.
The indicators may be distorted by labor-force exits, hidden price-control costs, and lack of productivity growth
after.feedback: Headline indicators can mislead. Falling unemployment may reflect labor-force exits, capped prices may hide shortages, and flat productivity weakens long-run living standards.

before.q: A scenario mentions scarcity and opportunity cost. What makes analysis integrated?
options: It uses scarcity to identify the forgone next-best alternative
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A scenario mentions scarcity and opportunity cost. What makes analysis integrated?
options: It uses scarcity to identify the forgone next-best alternative
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice, and opportunity cost identifies the value of the next-best alternative given up. Connecting those two ideas turns vocabulary recognition into economic reasoning.

before.q: A policy changes incentives and marginal benefits. What reasoning is required?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare the changed marginal benefit and cost created by incentives
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A policy changes incentives and marginal benefits. What reasoning is required?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare the changed marginal benefit and cost created by incentives
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: The policy changes incentives, which changes expected marginal benefits or costs. The behavioral prediction comes from comparing those changed marginal benefits and marginal costs.

before.q: A PPF move is described. What connection should be made?
options: Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
The slope or tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A PPF move is described. What connection should be made?
options: Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
The slope or tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: Movement along a PPF shows a production tradeoff. The slope or quantities given up reveal the opportunity cost of producing more of the other good.

before.q: A market failure is identified. What policy step remains?
options: Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Compare feasible remedies and their tradeoffs
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A market failure is identified. What policy step remains?
options: Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Compare feasible remedies and their tradeoffs
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: Identifying a market failure does not automatically identify the best remedy. Policy analysis must compare feasible interventions, their benefits, costs, and possible unintended consequences.

before.q: A policy claim mixes prediction and advice. What should be separated?
options: The positive effect claim and normative recommendation
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A policy claim mixes prediction and advice. What should be separated?
options: The positive effect claim and normative recommendation
Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: The prediction about what the policy will do is a positive claim that can be tested. The recommendation about what should be done is normative and depends on values as well as evidence.

before.q: Two producers specialize. What completes the reasoning?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare opportunity costs and feasible terms of trade
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: Two producers specialize. What completes the reasoning?
options: Simply repeat both vocabulary words
Compare opportunity costs and feasible terms of trade
Choose the most familiar concept and ignore the other
Assume mentioning policy automatically completes analysis
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: Specialization should follow comparative advantage, which requires comparing opportunity costs. For both sides to gain from exchange, the terms of trade must fall between their opportunity costs.

before.q: A worker receives a 4 percent nominal wage increase while consumer prices rise 6 percent. What bridge calculation is needed before judging living standards?
options: Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.
before.commonError: Evaluating purchasing power from nominal wages without adjusting for inflation.
before.feedback: Approximate real wage growth equals nominal wage growth minus inflation: 4 - 6 = -2 percent.

after.q: A worker receives a 4 percent nominal wage increase while consumer prices rise 6 percent. What calculation is needed before judging the change in living standards?
options: Add wage and price growth to obtain a 10 percent real gain.
Adjust the wage for inflation; the real wage fell about 2 percent.
Use the unemployment rate as the wage deflator.
Compare the nominal wage only with nominal GDP.
after.commonError: Evaluating purchasing power from nominal wages without adjusting for inflation.
after.feedback: Approximate real wage growth equals nominal wage growth minus inflation: 4 - 6 = -2 percent.

before.q: Limited resources force a city to choose projects. Which ideas connect?
options: The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Scarcity creates an opportunity cost equal to the best forgone project
One concept alone resolves every part of bridge 1
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: Limited resources force a city to choose projects. Which ideas connect?
options: The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Scarcity creates an opportunity cost equal to the best forgone project
Opportunity cost is unrelated to scarcity once the city has chosen a project.
after.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
after.feedback: Scarcity means the city cannot fund every project. Choosing one project therefore creates an opportunity cost equal to the value of the best forgone alternative.

before.q: A bonus changes effort until added benefit no longer exceeds added cost. Which ideas connect?
options: No causal or tradeoff connection is required
One concept alone resolves every part of bridge 2
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary
Incentives alter behavior evaluated at the margin
before.commonError: Matching vocabulary without combining causal reasoning.
before.feedback: Integrated analysis connects mechanisms from multiple concepts to reach one conclusion.

after.q: A bonus changes effort until added benefit no longer exceeds added cost. Which ideas connect?
options: No causal or tradeoff connection is required
Incentives determine behavior without any need to compare marginal benefits and costs.
The concepts are related only because they share vocabulary

options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice

after.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

before.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. What is the repair?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue

Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
before.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

after.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
Accounting profit ignores explicit costs
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
after.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

before.q: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. What is the repair?
options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs

before.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal

after.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

before.q: For the next worker, a orchard estimates 4 additional crates at $12 each. Compare that contribution with the $50 hourly wage.
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead

Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
before.commonError: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
before.feedback: The worker's VMP is $48 per hour (4 × $12). Because $48 is below $50, the worker costs more than the added output value.
